sentences.text: Invictarx is distinguished by osteoderms with a smooth surface texture, abundant random pits, and few or no neurovascular grooves. The animal likely possessed a co-ossified pelvic shield made of uniformly sized polygonal osteoderms, similar to Nodosaurus and Stegopelta. Some of Invictarx's cervical or pectoral osteoderms were up to 1.8 cm thick at their base and thinned to 0.6 cm at the edges. The keel on certain Invictarx osteoderms measured 2.2 cm thick before thinning down to just 0.6 cm. The most complete thoracic osteoderm found in the holotype specimen was only 5.1 cm wide. One of Invictarx's cervical osteoderms features a keel that is strongly offset to the side, similar to the genus Edmontonia.

The genus was named and described in 2018 by paleontologists Andrew T. McDonald and Douglas G. Wolfe. The genus name for this animal is Invictarx. The specific name of this animal is zephyri, making its full scientific name Invictarx zephyri.

The first fossil specimen was discovered in May 2011 by Daniel Williamson in the upper Allison Member of the Menefee Formation in the San Juan Basin. Two additional specimens were found in October 2011 by Andrew T. McDonald and in October 2015 by Keith Brockmann. In May 2011, Dan Williamson discovered an ankylosaur skeleton in San Juan County, New Mexico. Invictarx fossils were found in the upper part of the Allison Member of the Menefee Formation.

The only known species, Invictarx zephyri, is represented by three isolated and incomplete postcranial skeletons. The holotype includes six complete or nearly complete osteoderms, a dorsal rib, and additional osteoderm fragments.

The preserved vertebrae are identified as middle dorsal vertebrae based on comparisons with Sauropelta and Europelta, but they lack fused ribs. The neural canal in the vertebrae is ellipse-shaped with its axis oriented toward the upper edge and sides. The ulnar condyle of the forearm was larger than the radial condyle.

Invictarx is classified as a monospecific genus within the nodosaurid dinosaur family. Invictarx belongs to the parent group Nodosauridae. The family of Invictarx is Nodosauridae. Invictarx is classified in the class Ornithischia. Invictarx zephyri is the only known species of the extinct genus Invictarx, an ornithischian dinosaur belonging to the family Nodosauridae.

Invictarx is a monospecific genus of nodosaurid dinosaur that lived in New Mexico during the Late Cretaceous, specifically the lower Campanian stage around 78.5 million years ago. Invictarx lived during the lower Campanian stage, approximately 78.5 million years ago. Fossils of Invictarx have been found in New Mexico, USA, in rocks dating to the early Campanian stage of the Late Cretaceous. Invictarx lived during the Campanian stage, between 83.6 and 72.2 million years ago.

Invictarx inhabited a widespread alluvial floodplain environment characterized by mudstone, siltstone, sandstone, and coal. Invictarx lived alongside various dinosaurs including the tyrannosaurid Dynamoterror, the ceratopsid Menefeeceratops, the hadrosaurid Ornatops, and a dromaeosaurid similar to Saurornitholestes. Contemporary non-dinosaur animals included the alligatoroids Brachychampsa and Deinosuchus, as well as various indeterminate turtles.
